heading: One click per digit
body: A rotary phone had no buttons. Turn the dial to a digit, let it go, and on the way back it opened and closed the line once per unit, ten times a second. A 2 sent two clicks. A 0 sent ten. Switching equipment counted the clicks, so every click was time the equipment spent on your call.

heading: Five clicks to New York
body: In October 1947 AT&T assigned the first area codes. New York City got 212: two, one, two, five clicks, the fastest code on the plan. The usual account is that the busiest destinations got the shortest codes to save switch time. Some dispute that was the stated reason; the pattern in the assignments is there either way.

heading: The fastest four
body: Chicago got 312 and Los Angeles 213, six clicks each. Detroit got 313, seven. Pittsburgh's 412 took seven too. The big industrial cities of 1947 sit at the bright end of the scale.

heading: Seventy-seven codes
body: The plan gave the United States 77 codes, and Canada nine more. Here they fill in from the fastest to the slowest. Most of the country took between twelve and twenty clicks to reach.

heading: The slow end
body: South Dakota's 605, South Carolina's 803 and western North Carolina's 704 each took 21 clicks: four times New York. Montana, New Mexico, Vermont, Tennessee and northern Virginia took 20.

heading: A 0 in the middle means the whole state
body: The middle digit was a flag. Only area codes had a 0 or 1 there, so the equipment could tell a long-distance code from a local exchange. A 0 meant the code covered a whole state, like Florida's 305. A 1 meant the state was split, like the four Texas codes. 35 of the 77 were whole states.

heading: The first splits
body: The format allowed 152 codes. The first split came in 1948, when 219 was cut out of Indiana's 317. By 1960 the country carried 101 codes. Each new territory flashes as it appears.

heading: Running out of numbers
body: Growth used the plan up. Territories kept splitting, and from 1992 new codes were laid over old ones instead of dividing them: 917 over Manhattan was the first. Hatching marks those overlays. The last boundary split was 575 out of New Mexico's 505 in 2007.

heading: Today
body: By 2025 the lower 48 states carry 367 geographic codes on 237 territories, and eleven territories carry three or more. Houston's 713 territory holds five. The 1947 shape still shows through: 212 is still Manhattan, 313 is still Detroit.

heading: The pattern, in numbers
body: Clicks against the 1950 population of each territory, for all 77 originals. The fastest codes went to the most people; the slowest to the fewest. The method section has the data behind this chart.

heading: Explore
body: Pick a palette, drag the year, and switch the coloring between clicks, middle digit and the year each code arrived. Hover any territory for its codes and its 1947 ancestor. The view lives in the link, so you can copy one and send it.
